newsitem.title: USA: Officials say lower growth expected in SW Penn.
newsitem.headline: Officials say lower growth expected in SW Penn.

text.p: Planning officials in southwest Pennsylvania are forecasting much lower growth for the region than predicted just two years ago, when they devised an aggressive infrastructure improvement plan for the area.

Robert Kochanowski, executive director of the Southwestern Pennsylvania Regional Planning Commission (SPRPC), told Reuters population growth will be 3.3 percent and employment growth will be 9.1 percent over the next 20 years for the six-county region, which includes metropolitan Pittsburgh and surrounding rural areas.
Those figures are sharply lower than forecasts SPRPC made in November 1994, when officials devised an extensive highway and transit system improvement plan.
That plan was based on expectations of population growth of 17 percent and employment growth of 28 percent over the next two decades.

The SPRPC consists of commissioners from the six counties and federal, state, and local transportation and development officials. The group serves as the planning organization for the region and serves a central role in directing federal transportation funding.

The forecasts call for the leading job creator in the region through the year 2020 to be miscellaneous business services, predicted to grow by 56 percent. Those services include advertising, credit reporting, mailing, stenography, and others.

But the region's current largest employment sector, retail, is expected to decline by 15 percent in the same period, entailing a loss of 24,609 jobs through 2020. Employment losses also are expected in the primary metals, industrial machinery and banking industries.

"These latest forecasts are now saying we don't anticipate the levels of population and employment growth...I talked about a couple of years ago," Kochanowski said. "The model is now saying that at best growth will be almost level."
The computer model SPRPC uses is the Regional Economic Models Inc system, a nationally recognized program for predicting a region's growth level.

But Kochanowski said there is still room for transportation improvement in the face of diminished growth expectations. "You've got to have some progress to improve things or the region is going to continue to stagnate," he said.
Tim Parks, president of the Pittsburgh Regional Alliance, said the new figures are "a little conservative."
The Pittsburgh Regional Alliance is charged with marketing the region, retaining existing businesses and encouraging the start-up of new enterprises.
"I'm not suggesting there's going to be a boom," he said. "But the figures might be a little more robust."

Parks said several information technology companies have started up in the region in the past several years and he expects further growth with the start-up of more such businesses. "I think that the growth in information technology is being underestimated (by the model,") he said.

Moreover, Allegheny County Commissioner Larry Dunn said the new forecasts should be considered with caution because the region's tax structure has improved recently. "We have really dramatically changed things (with tax cuts,") he said. "So whatever growth projections there are, I want to make sure (those are taken into consideration.")
The forecasts have critics saying the region should scrap planned large-scale transportation projects, including a new airport busway and new traffic expressways.

"(The forecasts) totally undermine the projects...there is no need to create infrastructure to take care of (growth) which isn't going to exist," said David Tessitor, project director of American Town and Country Alliance, a non-profit group opposed to suburban sprawl.
Recent predictions from state officials have a less-than-rosy outlook for the entire state.
Robert Bittenbender, Gov. Tom Ridge's budget secretary, at a recent budget briefing predicted that Pennsylvania's economy will probably grow next year by just 1.1 percent.

That prediction was based on projections from Wharton Econometric Forecasting Associates, an economic consulting firm. That growth rate would mark the lowest economic growth rate in the past 20 years, except in those years when there was a recession.
Bittenbender also predicted that the state's unemployment rate would rise from about 5 percent now to 6.5 percent by early 1998.
